content: Workplace safety and health programs in coal liquefaction pilot plants are similar to those implemented in petroleum refineries and the chemical industry. These facilities typically have written procedures to ensure operational safety. These include protocols for locking out electrical equipment, tagging out valves, organizing fire and rescue brigades, issuing safe work permits, granting vessel entry permits, and mandating the use of safety glasses and hard hats. Housekeeping practices are also emphasized. Developers of occupational safety and health programs should rely on several resources: 1. General industry standards outlined in the Code of Federal Regulations (29 CFR Part 1910). 2. Voluntary guidelines from similar industries. 3. Recommendations from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) regarding specific work practices for similar materials. 4. Guidance from equipment manufacturers. 5. Professional judgment and operational experience. Employers must ensure that workers are informed about the hazards associated with materials present in the workplace, the procedures for handling these materials, cleaning up spills, and the proper use of personal protective equipment (PPE) and emergency protocols. Oral instructions should be supplemented with written and audiovisual materials to keep workers updated on the latest safety procedures and techniques. Additionally, workers' comprehension of these instructions should be regularly evaluated. Operating Procedures Coal liquefaction pilot plants are developing detailed procedures for every phase of operation, including startup, normal operation, routine maintenance, normal shutdown, emergency shutdown, and extended shutdowns. These procedures should address the safe storage of process materials, prevention of solidification of dissolved coal, cleanup of spills, and decontamination of equipment requiring maintenance. During the startup of high-pressure coal liquefaction systems, preventing leaks is a significant challenge. Systems should be gradually pressurized and inspected for leaks, particularly at valve outlets, blinds, and flanges. Recently repaired, serviced, or replaced equipment must be carefully examined. If no leaks are detected, the system should be slowly brought to operating pressure and temperature. If leaks are found, appropriate repairs must be made. High-pressure equipment should undergo routine inspections to determine maintenance needs. Monitoring and replacement intervals for equipment susceptible to erosion and corrosion should be established as part of a quality assurance program. Confined Space Entry NIOSH has provided recommendations for confined space entry in coal liquefaction facilities. These include entry permits, atmospheric testing, continuous monitoring, medical surveillance, personnel training, proper labeling and posting, and preparations such as isolation, lockout, tagout, purging, and ventilation. Safety equipment, clothing, and rescue equipment must also be available, and detailed recordkeeping is essential. One facility visited by NIOSH recommends an air changeover rate of six times per hour during entry and work in confined spaces. Restricted Areas Access to coal liquefaction plants should be controlled to prevent entry by individuals unfamiliar with the hazards, necessary precautions, and emergency procedures. At one facility, access is managed using warning signs, red lights, and barriers. In smaller facilities, physical barriers such as doors are feasible, while larger operations may use fences and gates. Employers should maintain a log of workers entering restricted areas to track exposure during high-risk operations. Visitor logs can also help account for individuals during accidents or emergencies. Visitors must be informed of hazards, necessary precautions, and emergency procedures. Spill Decontamination Toxic liquid spills should be cleaned up as soon as it is safe to do so. Equipment should be designed to contain spills and leaks with minimal worker exposure. Small spills can be managed using absorbents, which must then be disposed of safely. If manual cleanup is required, only trained and instructed workers should perform and supervise the process. Employers must provide appropriate PPE and ensure workers understand its use. Dried tar is particularly difficult to remove, so easily strippable coatings may be applied in areas prone to tar spills. These coatings allow for easier removal of tar along with the coating itself, leaving a clean surface that can be recoated. In plants where such coatings are not used, manual scraping, commercial cleaners, or steam may be employed, though these methods increase risks to cleanup personnel. For example, steam stripping can generate airborne contaminants and increase the risk of burns. Therefore, steam stripping is discouraged. When organic solvents are used for cleanup, exposure to solvent vapors and aerosols must be minimized through local ventilation and the use of approved respirators. Contaminated hand tools and portable equipment should be cleaned before reuse, using methods such as steam cleaning in enclosed systems, vapor degreasing, or ultrasonic agitation. Residues must be contained and disposed of properly, and solvents must be carefully controlled. Personal Hygiene When engineering controls are insufficient to prevent exposure, workers must remain vigilant about the potential hazards of direct contact with coal-derived products. They should practice good personal hygiene by: 1. Avoiding touching their faces, genitals, or rectal areas without first washing their hands. 2. Washing skin with soap and water after direct contact with coal-derived products. 3. Washing their hands, forearms, face, and neck after completing operations involving known or suspected contact with coal-derived products. Workers should also monitor for sores that do not heal, dead skin, and changes in warts or moles. Any suspicious lesions should be reported immediately to the medical department, as they may be early signs of cancer. To maintain good hygiene, workers must take showers at the end of each shift.
